items.bodyEn: Kawasaki was among the last post towns added to the Tōkaidō, in 1623, to break the long stretch between Shinagawa and Kanagawa. Travelers crossed the Tama River here on the Rokugō ferry: Ieyasu's bridge of 1600 washed away in the flood of 1688, and no bridge stood again until 1874. Hiroshige's Kawasaki print shows the ferry, Fuji behind.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō 1833–34: Kawasaki Rokugō Ferry; Shinpen Musashi fudoki

items.bodyEn: Kawasaki's specialty was Nara chameshi, rice simmered in tea with beans, served with tofu soup at the teahouse Mannen-ya near the ferry landing. Jippensha Ikku's comic road novel Tōkaidōchū Hizakurige (1802–14) has its heroes Yaji and Kita stop in Kawasaki for a bowl, and pilgrims bound for the temple Kawasaki Daishi kept the town's inns busy.
items.sourceNote: Jippensha Ikku, Tōkaidōchū Hizakurige (1802–14), Kawasaki episode

items.bodyEn: 片 means 'one side, a fragment', and katakana are just that: pieces broken off kanji. ア is the left side of 阿, イ the left of 伊, カ the 力 of 加. Heian-period monks jotted them between the lines of Chinese Buddhist texts as quick reading aids, which is why they stayed angular. Today they carry loanwords: コーヒー, タクシー.
items.sourceNote: Kōjien; Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, entry 片仮名

items.bodyEn: Small っ is never said on its own. It is a one-beat pause that doubles the next consonant: き・っ・て (stamp) has three beats, き・て (come) two. Katakana uses ッ the same way, and the long bar ー adds a beat to a vowel, so コーヒー is four beats. Keep every beat even; Japanese rhythm is counted, not stressed.
